UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al. 
 
) 
Docket No. EL25-49-000 
 
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating 
Facilities 
) 
Docket No. AD24-11-000 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC 
 
v. 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
 
) 
 
) 
Docket No. EL25-20-000 
(consolidated) 
 
ANSWER OF THE INDICATED PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS TO THE MOTION 
FOR EXPEDITED ACTION OF CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC  
 
Pursuant to Rule 2131 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”), the Indicated PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
(“PJM”) Transmission Owners (“Indicated TOs”)2 submit this Answer to the Motion for Expedited 
Action that was filed by Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) on November 
21, 2025 (“Constellation’s Motion”).3 
 
1  
See 18 C.F.R. § 385.213(d)(1) (“Any answer to a motion or to an amendment to a motion must be made within 
15 days after the motion or amendment is filed, except as described below or unless otherwise ordered.”). 
2  
This filing was prepared on behalf of the following PJM Transmission Owners: AMP Transmission, LLC; City 
of Cleveland, Department of Public Utilities, Division of Cleveland Public Power; City of Hamilton, OH; 
Duquesne Light Company; East Kentucky Power Cooperative; Exelon Corporation, on behalf of Atlantic City 
Electric Company, Baltimore Gas and Electric Company, Commonwealth Edison Company, Commonwealth 
Edison Company of Indiana, Inc., Delmarva Power & Light Company, PECO Energy Company, and Potomac 
Electric Power Company; FirstEnergy Service Company, as agent for its affiliates American Transmission 
Systems, Incorporated, Jersey Central Power & Light Company, Mid-Atlantic Interstate Transmission LLC, 
Keystone Appalachian Transmission Company, The Potomac Edison Company, Monongahela Power Company 
and Trans-Allegheny Interstate Line Company (collectively, the “FirstEnergy Transmission Companies”); Old 
Dominion Electric Cooperative; PPL Electric Utilities Corporation; Rockland Electric Company; Southern 
Maryland Electric Cooperative, Inc.; UGI Utilities Inc; and Wabash Valley Power Association, Inc. 
3  
Constellation attached its comments filed in Docket No. RM26-4-000 to its motion in this proceeding.  The 
Indicated TOs are not addressing all of the issues with the RM26-4-000 filing in the instant filing—those issues 
will instead be addressed where they belong in Docket No. RM26-4-000.

2 
 
For the reasons discussed herein, the Commission should reject Constellation’s Motion, 
which if granted would result in affordability concerns for customers, market uncertainty, 
reliability risks, and a jurisdictional overreach on the part of the Commission.  Should the 
Commission decide to act in this proceeding prior to resolution of Docket No. RM26-4-000, the 
only action that should be taken, as the Indicated TOs have previously explained, is to terminate 
the above-captioned complaint dockets because the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“PJM 
Tariff”) has not been shown to be unjust and unreasonable.4 
I. 
BACKGROUND 
On October 23, 2025, the Secretary (“Energy Secretary”) of the U.S. Department of Energy 
(“DOE”) “direct[ed] [FERC] to initiate rulemaking procedures and [to] consider [an] Advance 
Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANOPR) presenting potential reforms to ensure the timely and 
orderly interconnection of large loads to the transmission system.”5  The Energy Secretary 
submitted the proposal through his authority under section 403 of the Department of Energy 
Organization Act6 and asked that the Commission act on the proposal “no later than April 30, 
2026.”7  On October 27, 2025, the Commission issued a notice inviting comments on the ANOPR 
in a new rulemaking docket, Docket No. RM26-4-000.8  Among other things, the ANOPR is 
exploring the possibility of standardizing interconnection procedures and agreements for “hybrid 
 
4  
See Answer of Indicated TOs at 24–25 (June 3, 2025). 
5  
Secretary Chris Wright, DOE, Ensuring the Timely and Orderly Interconnection of Large Loads: Advance Notice 
of Proposed Rulemaking (“ANOPR”), Docket No. RM26-4-000,  at P 1 (Oct. 27, 2025) (footnote omitted) (“DOE 
ANOPR Filing”). 
6  
See 42 U.S.C. § 7173(a) (“The Secretary and the Commission are authorized to propose rules, regulations, and 
statements of policy of general applicability with respect to any function within the jurisdiction of the Commission 
under section 7172 of this title.”). 
7  
DOE ANOPR Filing, Transmittal Letter at 2. 
8  
Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission System, Docket No. RM26-4-000, Notice Inviting 
Comments (Oct. 27, 2025).

3 
 
facilities,” which the ANOPR defines as loads, “seeking to share a point of interconnection with 
new or existing generation facilities.”9  Hundreds of comments and reply comments were 
submitted by numerous parties on the ANOPR.   
Constellation’s Motion asks that FERC quickly move forward and rule on co-located load 
issues in PJM, rather than waiting until it has considered and ruled in the aforementioned 
rulemaking proceeding.10 
II. 
ANSWER 
A. Constellation’s Desire for a PJM-Specific Outcome Is Inappropriate 
Where the Commission Is Evaluating These Issues at a National Level in 
the Pending ANOPR Proceeding. 
PJM’s existing tariff is just and reasonable and should be upheld for that reason.  Further, 
it would cause confusion and unwarranted expense and upheaval for the Commission to modify 
the PJM Tariff in this proceeding on an interim basis before addressing issues nationwide in 
Docket No. RM26-4-000.  Would an early ruling in PJM mean that PJM will have different rules 
from the rest of the country?  Or would the rules be changed again once a ruling is issued in RM26-
4-000?  Any changes to the PJM Tariff should be informed by the principles or rules established 
through the ANOPR process, to adhere to the policy direction and solutions, which FERC is now 
contemplating on a national basis.  A patchwork of rules that may or may not change in the near-
term is a recipe for market uncertainty that could stifle rather than assist sensible forward 
movement on data center development, including investment delays in energy infrastructure 
 
9  
DOE ANOPR Filing at P 12. 
10  Constellation’s Motion suggests transmission owners are delaying large load interconnections.  See 
Constellation’s Motion at 2.  Nothing could be further from the truth.  The Indicated TOs are fully supportive of 
interconnecting large loads, co-located or otherwise, as quickly, safely, equitably, and reliably as possible, 
consistent with the existing just and reasonable PJM Tariff and with applicable state laws.  Concurrently with this 
answer, Exelon is filing a separate answer to correct any misapprehension regarding the ability of large loads and 
their load serving entities to receive transmission services in the Exelon service territories.

4 
 
needed to support increasing demand.  The expedited action in this docket that Constellation seeks 
would potentially pre-judge issues to be decided in the ANOPR proceeding without adequate 
consideration of the full record being developed there and potentially result in conflicting 
outcomes.   
Constellation argues that an early ruling for PJM is supported by the fact that the DOE 
ANOPR Filing explains that it “is not intended in any way to discourage public utilities from 
making filings to address these and similar issues under [Federal Power Act (“FPA”)] section 
205.”11  But allowing filings under FPA section 20512 is simply a reflection of the statute—public 
utilities have a right under FPA section 205 “to file rates and terms for services rendered with 
[their] assets.”13  This reservation of rights to transmission owners to modify tariffs at any time for 
service provided with their assets does not alter the far stricter rules applicable to FPA section 
20614 actions, which can only proceed when the rate is found “unjust [and] unreasonable.”15  That 
burden has not been met, nor would it be appropriate to make such a finding while the hundreds 
of comments on the ANOPR are in the midst of their review.  Should the Commission decide to 
act in this proceeding prior to action in the ANOPR docket, as the Indicated TOs have explained 
in prior filings, the appropriate course of action would be to terminate the complaint and show 
cause proceedings for failure to meet the burden established under FPA section 206.16 
 
11  DOE ANOPR Filing at P 32. 
12  16 U.S.C. § 824d. 
13  Atl. City Elec. Co. v. FERC, 295 F.3d 1, 9 (D.C. Cir. 2002) (citing 16 U.S.C. § 824d). 
14  16 U.S.C. § 824e. 
15  Id. § 824e(a). 
16  See, e.g., Answer of Indicated TOs at 2–3 (June 3, 2025) (“Neither the Commission nor any of the parties 
supporting the initiation of this FPA section 206 proceeding have demonstrated that the existing [PJM Tariff] is 
unjust and unreasonable.  Consequently, the only action that may lawfully be taken is to terminate this 
proceeding.”).

5 
 
B. Constellation Would Have the Commission Improperly and Prematurely 
Make a Broad Jurisdictional Determination in this Proceeding. 
Under FPA section 201(b)(1), FERC has jurisdiction over “the transmission of electric 
energy in interstate commerce and . . . the sale of electric energy at wholesale in interstate 
commerce.”17  Except as otherwise provided for under the FPA, carved out from FERC’s 
jurisdiction are “facilities used for the generation of electric energy[,] . . . facilities used in local 
distribution or only for the transmission of electric energy in intrastate commerce, . . . [and] 
facilities for the transmission of electric energy consumed wholly by the transmitter.”18 
The National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissions (“NARUC”) recognizes in a 
recent resolution that “the ANOPR asserts FERC jurisdiction over the interconnection of large 
loads to the transmission system” and asks FERC to “make clear that it is affirmatively not 
asserting jurisdiction over end-use sales, which falls squarely within the exclusive jurisdiction of 
state retail energy regulatory authorities.”19 
In the Show Cause Order in this proceeding, FERC explained that, 
[T]he Commission has exercised authority over the terms of certain 
interconnections to the transmission system as “an essential element 
of [t]ransmission [s]ervice.”  Although the Commission reached that 
conclusion based on the nature of interconnection to the 
transmission system generally, not the purpose for such 
interconnection (i.e., to make a wholesale sale or to make a 
wholesale or retail purchase), it has not historically exercised

18  Id. 
19  NARUC, EL-1 Resolution Urging the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to Preserve and Affirm State Retail 
Regulatory Jurisdiction in its Large Load Interconnection Proceeding, Substantive Resolutions Passed by the 
NARUC Board of Directors, at 6, https://pubs.naruc.org/pub/97FE08D1-CF4D-9199-BA7F-
5884DD427E55?_gl=1*1cgs1pd*_ga*MTEwMTgwNTA4OS4xNzUxNTQ3Nzc0*_ga_QLH1N3Q1NF*czE3
NjI5NTMxNTAkbzExJGcxJHQxNzYyOTUzMTY4JGo0MiRsMCRoMA (adopted by the NARUC Board of 
Directors on Nov. 11, 2025).

6 
 
jurisdiction over any and all transmission-level interconnections of 
retail load.20      
 
The Commission further explained that it has “examine[d] whether certain facilities had a 
‘dual use,’ (i.e., the facilities were used for both wholesale and retail purposes), but the 
Commission limited its assertion of jurisdiction to distribution level interconnections.”21  And in 
another recent proceeding, FERC declined to address “jurisdiction over the process of 
interconnecting loads to the Commission-jurisdictional transmission system.”22 
Constellation would have the Commission decide in this proceeding that co-located load 
interconnections should be treated as entirely FERC-jurisdictional, disregarding the fact that retail 
service to the loads is definitely not subject to FERC authority.  Consistent with their prior 
comments,23 the Indicated TOs reiterate that it is the Network Integration Transmission Service 
(“Network Service”) customer that is taking FERC-jurisdictional transmission service in serving 
the co-located load, which is typically a load serving entity, but if a state allows, it may be the load 
itself.  The only part of such an arrangement that is FERC jurisdictional is the transmission service 
provided by the interstate grid to the load serving entity. 
The Commission may decide, to the extent it has jurisdiction, how transmission costs 
associated with large load customer interconnections will be recovered in FERC Docket No. 
RM26-4-000.  In the context of this proceeding, for FERC to determine what transmission costs

(“Show Cause Order”); see also id. PP 66–72. 
21  Id. P 72 n.224 (citation omitted). 
22   Tri-State Generation and Transmission Ass’n, Inc., 193 FERC ¶ 61,070, at P 50 (2025)  (“Because it appears that 
Tri-State’s proposal before us sets the terms of retail sales, we need not elaborate in this order on other matters

interconnecting loads to the Commission-jurisdictional transmission system.”). 
23  See Answer of Indicated TOs at 15–16 (June 3, 2025).

7 
 
should appear on a particular retail customer’s (including a large load customer’s) bill would have 
FERC tread into questionable jurisdictional territory that would have broad national implications. 
Notably, Network Service addresses many of the jurisdictional issues raised by NARUC 
and others.  That is, there are no jurisdictional complications if loads are served by a state-
authorized load serving entity that procures Network Service to serve that load and, perhaps, other 
loads.  Affirmation by FERC that this is Network Service, and that FERC has jurisdiction over that 
service, will clarify the contentious jurisdictional debate.  Once it is made clearer that this service 
is Network Service, the process for seeking service is unambiguous under the existing PJM Tariff 
and has not been shown to be a problem.  Of course, network customers have to pay for embedded 
costs of transmission—something Constellation objects to—but that has not been shown to be 
unjust and unreasonable. 
C. Constellation’s Preferred Outcome Raises Significant Affordability and 
Reliability Concerns. 
What Constellation proposes would result in large loads avoiding their share of the cost of 
the transmission services that they rely upon.  But the services are not free.  If the large loads do 
not pay for the transmission system and related services that they use, someone else must pay 
instead.  Constellation’s continued push to subsidize co-located load would result in significant 
cost-shifts to other customers.24 
While transmission and ancillary service charges are the primary issue in this proceeding, 
load impacts should certainly be taken into consideration.  PJM’s independent market monitor, 
Monitoring Analytics, LLC, warned in its recent 2025 Quarterly State of the Market Report that 
rapid data center growth is driving tight supply-demand conditions, higher capacity prices, and 
 
24  See Exelon Comments in Opposition to Complaint, Docket No. EL25-20, at Attach. 2, Declaration of John J. 
Reed & Danielle S. Powers (filed Dec. 12, 2024).

8 
 
increased transmission and energy costs for all customers.25  The Market Report asserts that 
proposals to let data centers remove existing capacity from the market and dedicate it to themselves 
would create cost shifts and reliability risks until new generation is built.26  Constellation’s Motion 
not only evades this issue entirely but attempts to sidestep regulatory and PJM oversight of the 
issue by not measuring the actual consumption of large loads that the grid must be prepared to 
support. 
Increased transmission investment will be needed to ensure continued reliability of the grid 
when massive and diverse new loads become connected to the system.  The lack of visibility into 
the operation of these loads, as discussed further below, could adversely affect grid stability and 
prevent adequate planning on the part of PJM.  This underscores the proposition that new large 
loads, whether or not co-located with generation, should pay their share of the embedded cost of 
the transmission system. 
As PJM’s independent market monitor explained, it would be inappropriate to “shift the 
costs of serving data center load to all other customers.”27  But that is exactly what would happen 
if Constellation’s plan were to go forward, permitting data centers to receive the benefits of the 
electric grid without bearing their fair share of costs for that service.  Constellation’s proposal to 
allow certain categories of customers to avoid paying for transmission service would only frustrate 
the purpose of the FPA, which is “to encourage the orderly development of plentiful supplies of 
electricity . . . at reasonable prices.”28   
 
25  Monitoring Analytics, LLC, Q3 State of the Market Report for PJM: January Through September, at 1–3 (Nov. 
13, 2025), https://www.monitoringanalytics.com/reports/PJM_State_of_the_Market/2025/2025q3-som-pjm.pdf 
(“Market Report”). 
26  See id. 
27  Id. at 3. 
28  NAACP v. FPC, 425 U.S. 662, 669–70 (1976).

9 
 
Affordability should remain top of mind for the Commission.  In PJM, demand has 
outpaced the development of supply.29  The transmission system requires maintenance to ensure 
reliability, resilience, and quality of service.  Maintenance comes at a cost, and all customers that 
benefit from that maintenance and that rely upon the transmission system should bear that cost.  
Doing otherwise would place disproportionate financial risks on an ongoing basis to other 
customers and unduly benefit large loads that avoid paying for Network Service.   
Another problem is visibility by transmission system operators and planners into critical 
information and operating conditions that bear on system stability and reliability.  When co-located 
load is hidden and not appropriately accounted for in transmission planning and operations, it 
creates reliability risks by undermining accurate system modeling and resource adequacy 
assessments.  North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) has explained in this 
proceeding that (1) “system operators may lack sufficient information to perform reliability 
analysis on co-located large loads”; (2) “large loads may or may not be visible to system operators 
depending on the load’s operation and interconnection type”; (3) “[i]f a load is connected but

particularly in areas where data center development is occurring. . . . Most assessment areas are projecting an

demand forecasts continue to rise.”); id. at 92 (“Overall, new generation is coming on-line slower than anticipated. 
Generator retirements are outpacing the new generation replacing them.  As a result, PJM could face future 
resource adequacy challenges, impacting system reliability and PJM’s ability to serve load. PJM could be at risk 
of facing resource adequacy challenges if these trends continue.  PJM has applied an 11% reduction to the

generation.”); id. at 93 (“Driven by discrete and localized load growth, like Data Center Alley in Loudoun County, 
Virginia, in 2022, PJM and stakeholders conducted a review of data center load growth and identified growth 
rates of over 300% in some instances.”).

10 
 
operating conditions are providing only partial or no generation, there is a risk of thermal overloads 
and voltage or stability issues”; and (4) “[f]luctuations from large loads during faults or switching 
can cause issues with voltage support, frequency response, stability, and protection system 
coordination.”30  
In other words, behind-the-meter loads “can pose reliability risks if their generation 
unexpectedly trips off-line and appropriate protection or ride-through systems are not in place 
[because] [t]he operational visibility and controllability of [behind-the-meter] loads are limited, 
making it more challenging to predict system impacts, especially during uncontrolled transitions 
between on-site generation and grid supply that may arise due to protection system failures.”31  “If 
the load unexpectedly shifts to expecting grid supply after the co-located generation fails, the 
utility supply sees a rapid demand spike, which may stress the transmission system.”32 
Increased demand without appropriate planning due to hidden load will result in 
transmission and generation constraints.  Large loads that are not visible as part of the PJM 
planning process can very well deplete transmission and generation capacity in times of increased 
demand.  The effect will be increased costs and decreased quality of service for other customers.  
The way to mitigate this is by maintaining the requirement for these large co-located loads to be 
subject to Network Service and the costs that should attend that service.

11 
 
D. Nothing Has Changed: The Standard Under Federal Power Act Section 
206 Has Not Been Met. 
As a legal matter, nothing has changed since the commencement of this proceeding.  As 
discussed in the prior submissions of the Indicated TOs, the existing forms of transmission service 
in PJM—Network Service and Point-to-Point Transmission Service (“PTP Service”)—continue to 
be just and reasonable methods of providing transmission service to loads in PJM, including loads 
co-located with generation facilities.   
Constellation continues to ignore a fundamental part of FPA section 206:33 only after a 
successful showing that the existing rate is unjust and unreasonable can the Commission order a 
replacement rate.34  No such showing has been made.  The PJM Tariff remains just and reasonable, 
and nothing in the record of this proceeding proves otherwise.  “The burden of proving an unjust 
or unreasonable rate rests with the party that initiated the proceeding—that is, the Commission or 
the third-party complainant.”35  Neither the Commission nor any of the parties supporting the 
initiation of this FPA section 206 proceeding have demonstrated that the existing PJM Tariff forms 
of transmission service are unjust and unreasonable.  The indisputable fact is that there is a path 
under the existing PJM Tariff for all customers to get service in a timely fashion at reasonable, 
non-preferential rates.  
The two options for transmission service under the PJM Tariff—Network Service and PTP 
Service—allow for recovery of the embedded costs of the PJM grid.36  Constellation seeks to

exempt large co-located loads from these costs, granting undue preference at the expense of other 
customers, contrary to the FPA’s mandate that all rates be just and reasonable and free from undue 
discrimination.37 
Co-located loads rely on the transmission system for essential services and impose 
reliability challenges.  As the Indicated TOs have previously explained,38 the “assessment of 
[Network Integration Transmission Service] is not based on actual use over a particular 
transmission path, but rather based on the network customer’s right to use the entire system”39 and 
its effects on that system.  Preferential treatment cannot be justified under the guise of national 
security, as similar critical facilities that contribute to our national security already pay under the 
existing PJM Tariff.  The real issue here is cost allocation and the attempt by some to shift to other 
customers the embedded costs of the transmission system. 
The outcome in Docket Nos. ER24-2172-000 and ER24-2172-001 (“Susquehanna ISA 
Proceeding”) illustrates this point.40  The proposal in that case was to avoid Network Service

through a behind-the-meter arrangement.41  That proposal sought essentially what Constellation 
seeks here, an exemption from responsibility for embedded costs.  The Commission rejected the 
proposal in the Susquehanna ISA Proceeding.42  What happened next is most instructive: the data 
center development continued anyway, and it did so under the existing Network Service option 
available under the PJM Tariff.43  Which is to say that nothing about the arrangement or the current 
PJM Tariff required the behind-the-meter form of service.  Constellation’s claim that the PJM Tariff 
is unjust and unreasonable is misplaced; no basis exists for creating a new service or replacement 
rate.44 
No matter how quickly any party prefers action in this proceeding, the Commission cannot 
order any replacement rates merely to accommodate the type of service some customers would 
prefer.  Again, FPA section 206 only permits action when the existing rate is unjust and 
unreasonable—which has not been shown.  Additionally, as the Indicated TOs have previously 
explained,45 Commission action to attempt to set a replacement rate that would accommodate a 
narrow category of customers, such as co-located load, would conflict with the major questions

doctrine46 and the declaration in the FPA that rates that provide an undue preference or advantage 
are unlawful.47  Congress could have given FERC authority to require preferred transmission 
service to benefit certain wholesale (or retail) customers, but it did not do so. 
III. 
Conclusion 
There are important issues to consider such as possible reforms to the interconnection 
queue process to minimize unjustified delays.  That is where the problem is—not with the type of 
transmission services offered.  Constellation wants to avoid paying for Network Service and asks 
for quick action to establish a new form of service in PJM to accommodate its desires while the 
Commission simultaneously considers related national policy direction and solutions.  There is no 
basis for that and the standard under FPA section 206 has not been met to require such a change 
to the PJM Tariff.  For the reasons stated above, FERC should reject Constellation’s Motion.  
Should FERC decide to act in this proceeding prior to resolution of the ANOPR proceeding, the 
complaint and show cause proceedings should be terminated, and FERC should find that the PJM 
Tariff remains just and reasonable.

Congress, and ‘enabling legislation’ is generally not an ‘open book to which the agency [may] add pages and 
change the plot line.’” (alteration in original (citation omitted))); see also Midship Pipeline Co., L.L.C. v. FERC, 
45 F.4th 867, 877 (5th Cir. 2022) (vacating part of the Commission’s order and remanding the remainder because 
“[t]he FERC’s interpretation of the NGA to give the agency power to determine ‘the reasonable cost’ of 
remediation efforts ‘change[d] the plot line’ of its enabling legislation, and was therefore erroneous” and “[t]he 
FERC lacks such  authority under the NGA, and it likewise lacked authority to order an ALJ to make such a 
determination indirectly” (second alteration in original (quoting West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. at 723))). 
47  See 16 U.S.C. § 824d(b).
